conflict_topics: unclean shared pan / responsibility for cleaning
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants speak in short, natural turns and raise concrete, household-level complaints (pan, smell, fan).
Some repetition of the same complaints (pan since last night; smell persists) across rounds without new proposals.
No explicit proposals for concrete solutions (e.g., who will clean, schedule, or ventilate longer) are offered.
evaluation.final_reason: No substantive agreement was reached by the end of the transcript. The shared pan with pork fat remained in the sink and no one accepted responsibility to clean it; A denied using the pan, B insisted the cooking smell is a problem and asked for ventilation, C demanded cleaning, and D requested to use the stove but was blocked by the pan. No party agreed to clean, move, or otherwise change behavior, so the incompatible practical states persisted.
position_change_notes: No participant changed their position during the run: A denied using the pan and maintained that ventilation was being used; B continued to complain about smell and requested ventilation; C consistently demanded cleaning; D consistently denied using the pan and sought to use the stove.
No one volunteered to clean the pan or accepted another's proposed action (there were effectively no proposals).

round_scores.evidence: C: "someone left pork in the shared pan. I can't use it now." D: "This is what I mean. Every night it's something." — Complaint about an unwashed shared pan and recurring problems appears for the first time.

A: "I cooked. The pan wasn't me." B: "The pan is one thing, but the smell from your cooking is the problem right now. ... Can you please use the fan and open the window?" — Denial of responsibility for the pan and an active demand (use fan/window) create a clearer interpersonal disagreement.

A: "They were. The fan is on and the window's open." B: "Well, it's not working. The whole place still smells." — Parties restate opposing claims about whether ventilation is being used/works; no settlement.

C: "The pan. It's been sitting there since last night. ... Who's going to clean it?" A: "Right? It's been there since last night." — The unwashed pan remains an explicit practical obstacle; responsibility is still contested/unaddressed.

C: "Who used it last?" D: "So is anyone going to use the stove? Or are we just going to talk about the pan?" — A practical incompatibility emerges: someone wants to use the stove but the shared pan blocks use; impatience increases and no one accepts responsibility.

A: "The shared pan is still there." D: "Right. And I didn't use it. So can I use the stove?" — The blocking problem persists; D requests use and denies responsibility but no one offers to move/clean the pan or sets a plan.

substantive_insights: The core tensions are practical (a shared, unwashed pan blocking stove use) and behavioral (cooking causing smells), not just differences in taste.
Lack of pre-agreed rules about shared kitchen responsibilities is driving recurring disputes and finger-pointing.
The immediate practical incompatibility (someone wants to cook now but the shared pan blocks the stove) escalates urgency beyond abstract complaints about smell.
